rows: 1, main p. 3
Start with the large movement, then the expanded fixation. Compare the small predicted rate change with the larger observed fluctuation in b. Read c as one cell and d as the population.
A weak, positive rate relationship exists during fixation. The large movement is used for calibration.
2, main p. 4

The spike response kernel in a has a delay and two decay times; b shows their spread. In c, a noisy cell prediction can coexist with a smooth eye trace. Panel d plots $R$, while e–f plot $\chi$ and estimation error.
Shared movement and a model-based fraction of common variance. The vertical axis in f is error in $\chi$, not eye position or another variance fraction. Large error cells receive little weight.
3, main p. 6
In a, distinguish the raw MSD, plateau estimate, and corrected curve. In b, compare both height and slope. Translating the private-noise curve upward does not remove its flattening.
Independent filtered motor noise fails both the amplitude and time dependence comparison. The noise subtraction is part of this evidence.
4, main p. 7

The valley in a sketches stable directions across the attractor and a neutral direction along it. It is not a measured energy function of this brain circuit. Panels c–d show simulated internal drift and its nearly linear MSD.
The mechanism by which neural noise can accumulate into an ordinary diffusive position signal. This is the integrator output before the full observation process.
5, main p. 8
Trace integrator, OMNs, plant, and feedback in a. Compare internal and actual position in c, then model and data MSD in d. Panels e–f rerun the statistical analysis on simulated recordings.

The full model can match filtered motion, and known simulated sources can produce noisy individual estimates with a useful population estimate. This checks the method under that model, rather than proving a unique biological source.
